sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Often asymptomatic until severe; peaked T waves and widened QRS on EKG may precede fatal arrhythmia; muscle weakness and ascending paralysis in severe cases — EKG is more important than symptoms in guiding urgency
Cardiac: bradycardia, irregular rhythm, hypotension, poor perfusion
Neuro / muscular: weakness, paresthesias, ascending flaccid paralysis in severe cases
Volume status: overload (JVD, crackles, edema) vs. dehydration / DKA
Signs of underlying cause: muscle tenderness / dark urine (rhabdomyolysis), fistula / dialysis catheter, hyperpigmentation or shock (adrenal crisis)
BRASH: Bradycardia + Renal failure + AV-nodal blocker + Shock + Hyperkalemia — may have profound bradycardia with only modest K elevation (5.5–6.2)

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Cr, bicarb, glucose), CBC, Mg, ABG/VBG if acidosis, CK if rhabdomyolysis, uric acid/phosphate if TLS, cortisol if adrenal insufficiency suspected
STEP 1: Membrane stabilization (calcium):** Give if ECG changes present (QRS widening, bradycardia, P-wave loss, sine wave, ventricular arrhythmia) or peri-arrest.
--**Calcium gluconate 3g IV** (30 mL of 10%) over ~10 min via peripheral IV — give periferally.
--OR **calcium chloride 1g IV** (10 mL of 10%) over ~5 min — preferred peri-arrest/resuscitation. NOTE: 1g CaCl₂ ≈ 3g calcium gluconate in elemental calcium — these are NOT equivalent doses.
--Recheck ECG in 10 min — repeat calcium if major changes persist. ** lasts only 30-60 min**; ECG toxicity can recur if K is not removed.
**Monitoring:** 12-lead ECG (K ≥6.0); telemetry (K ≥6.5 or ECG changes); fingerstick glucose q30-60 min × 2h then q1h × 6h after insulin; serial BMP q1-2h during active treatment
STEP 2: Shift K intracellularly:** **Regular insulin 10 units IV** + **dextrose 25g IV** (50 mL D50W or 250 mL D10W). Onset 10-20 min, peak ~30-60 min, lowers K ~0.6-1.0 mEq/L.
--Insulin dose adjustment: Use 5 units IV in ESRD, advanced CKD, low body weight, or high hypoglycemia risk — comparable K lowering with lower hypoglycemia rate in these populations.
--Albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized — additive to insulin, lowers K ~0.5-1.0 mEq/L. THIS IS NOT THE ASTHMA DOSE (2.5 mg). May be less effective in ESRD or patients on nonselective beta blockers.

--Sodium bicarbonate: NOT routine: no sugnifigant K decrease if pH normal (2025 ILCOR). Give only when metabolic acidosis is present; isotonic bicarb (150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1L D5W) preferred over hypertonic boluses when indicated.

--Balanced fluids (LR, Plasmalyte) not contraindicated even though has K. Large volume NS infusion can cause hyperchloremic acidosis, which may worsen K shift — consider LR/Plasmalyte in hypovolemic patients without a bicarbonate indication.
STEP 3 — Remove K from the body:**
--Loop diuretic: **furosemide 40-80 mg IV** (loop-naïve); 80-120 mg IV with advanced CKD or chronic loop exposure. An anuric patient cannot excrete K — do not pursue diuresis in anuria.
--**SZC (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) 10g PO TID × 48-72h** — useful elimination adjunct, onset hours UKKA recommends for K ≥6.0-6.5.
--Patiromer 8.4g PO — alternative binder; slower kinetics, less suitable for urgent hyperkalemia.
--Avoid SPS (Kayexalate) — slow, unpredictable, poor acute evidence, risk of bowel injury. UKKA has removed it from routine acute management.

**Dialysis**: prepare early for ESRD + K ≥6.5, anuric/oliguric patient with rising K, persistent K ≥6.5 despite medical therapy, severe AKI, massive ongoing K release (rhabdomyolysis, TLS), or refractory metabolic acidosis. Call nephrology before the 3rd round of insulin.
STEP 4 — Monitor:**

Glucose: q30-60 min × first 2h, then q1h through 6h after insulin. Hypoglycemia occurs in ~17% — median onset ~2h after treatment. If pre-treatment glucose <126 mg/dL, add D10W at 50 mL/hr × 5h after the insulin/dextrose bolus.

K: recheck **~1h** after treatment → 4h. Rebound hyperkalemia is expected when insulin/albuterol effects wear off unless K has been urinated, bound, or dialyzed out. A patient who looks fixed at 01:00 may have K 6.7 again at 05:00.
Repeat ECG after calcium + treatment if initial tracing was abnormal. Continue telemetry.
Track urine output — are kidneys actually removing k.
**Hold:** ACEi/ARB, K-sparing diuretics, TMP-SMX, NSAIDs, K supplements, TPN K, K in maintenance fluids.
Treat underlying cause: dialysis, relieve obstruction, treat DKA/acidosis, manage rhabdomyolysis or tumor lysis.

pairs.value: Bradycardia + Renal failure + AV-nodal blocker + Shock + Hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia and AV-nodal blockade synergize to produce profound bradycardia out of proportion to the K level.

Older CKD patient on metoprolol/carvedilol/diltiazem/verapamil, becomes dehydrated, septic, or develops AKI → K creeps up → HR 30-40 → CO falls → renal perfusion worsens → K worsens further. K may only be 5.5–6.2.
The bradycardia is not primarily from excessive vagal tone — it is from membrane toxicity + AV nodal drug effect. Atropine has limited effect in this physiology.

Stop the AV-nodal blocker. Treat hyperkalemia aggressively: calcium, insulin/dextrose, high-dose albuterol. Restore perfusion/volume if appropriate. Consider epinephrine for bradycardic shock. Promote kaliuresis if urine output allows. Dialysis if refractory.

K ≥6.5: ECG + telemetry, calcium for ECG changes, insulin/dextrose, albuterol 10-20 mg. Call dialysis immediately — do not waste time on aggressive diuresis in an anuric patient. SZC as adjunct while awaiting dialysis.

Serum K may be high with profoundly depleted total-body K. Treat the DKA. As insulin is started, K will fall rapidly — replace once serum K reaches appropriate range. Do not confuse initial hyperkalemia with total-body K excess.

Insulin temporarily improves the number while intracellular K continues pouring into circulation. These patients need aggressive management of the underlying process, frequent K measurements, appropriate volume management, early nephrology, and lower threshold for RRT if oliguric or K continues rising.

If the patient looks well, renal function is normal, ECG is normal, and K is unexpectedly 6.5 from a hemolyzed sample — redraw correctly. !!If the patient is bradycardic with wide QRS and K is 7.2 — do not spend 30 min debating hemolysis!!.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10%
drugs.notes: Preferred via peripheral IV. Membrane stabilization only — does NOT lower K. Onset 1-3 min, duration ~30-60 min. Repeat if ECG changes persist. 3g gluconate ≈ 1g CaCl₂ in elemental calcium — not equivalent.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.contraindications: Hypercalcemia; peripheral extravasation causes tissue injury
drugs.notes: Preferred peri-arrest/resuscitation. More elemental calcium per gram than gluconate. Use central line when feasible; peripheral acceptable in peri-arrest if no central access.

drugs.name: Regular insulin
drugs.dose: 10 units IV (5 units in ESRD/CKD/low weight/high hypoglycemia risk)
drugs.notes: Give with dextrose unless glucose >200-250. Lowers K ~0.6-1.0 mEq/L. Peak effect 30-60 min. Watch for delayed hypoglycemia esp. in CKD/ESRD — monitor glucose for 6h.

drugs.name: Dextrose 50% (D50W)
drugs.contraindications: Hyperglycemia without insulin coverage; extravasation risk
drugs.notes: Give with insulin. D10W 250 mL is equivalent. If pre-treatment glucose <126 mg/dL, add D10W drip at 50 mL/hr × 5h after bolus (UKKA 2026).

drugs.name: Albuterol
drugs.contraindications: Tachyarrhythmia (relative); hypokalemia risk at high doses
drugs.notes: THIS IS NOT THE ASTHMA DOSE — 2.5 mg neb is inadequate for hyperkalemia. Lowers K ~0.5-1.0 mEq/L. Additive with insulin. May be less effective in ESRD or on nonselective beta blockers. Watch for tachycardia.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.dose: 150 mEq in 1L D5W IV (isotonic); or 50-100 mEq IV bolus
drugs.contraindications: Alkalemia, hypernatremia, volume overload without acidosis indication
drugs.notes: NOT routine therapy — 2025 ILCOR found essentially no meaningful K reduction in normal-pH patients. Use when meaningful metabolic acidosis is present. Isotonic formulation preferred over hypertonic boluses.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.dose: 40-80 mg IV (loop-naïve); 80-160 mg IV with CKD/chronic loop use
drugs.contraindications: Anuria — loop diuretics cannot lower K in an anuric patient
drugs.notes: Definitive K removal via urine if kidneys are functioning. Assess volume status before/after. Dose for renal function and prior loop exposure.

drugs.name: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC)
drugs.dose: 10g PO TID × 48-72h, then 5-10g daily for maintenance
drugs.notes: Useful elimination adjunct. Onset hours — not for cardiac rescue. UKKA recommends for K ≥6.0-6.5. Watch for sodium load/edema in HF/CKD.

drugs.name: Patiromer
drugs.notes: GI K binder. Slower kinetics than SZC — less suitable for urgent hyperkalemia. Separate from other oral medications by ≥3h.

pairs.value: Mild: 5.5-5.9 | Moderate: 6.0-6.4 | Severe: ≥6.5 or any K with toxic ECG / hemodynamic instability.

pairs.key: Normal ECG does NOT rule out danger
pairs.value: ≥50% of patients with K ≥6.5 lack classic ECG findings. Peaked T waves occur in only ~**1/3** of moderate/severe cases. A normal ECG is reassuring but not safe to use as the sole determinant that a K of 6.8 is benign.

Bradycardia and conduction slowing (PR prolongation, P-wave flattening, QRS widening, sine wave) are more ominous than peaked T waves alone. Classic ECG progression: peaked T waves → PR/P-wave changes → QRS widening → sine wave → VT/VF/asystole.

1) Is it real? 2) Is the heart in danger? 3) Stabilize (calcium). 4) Shift (insulin/albuterol). 5) Remove K (diuresis/binder/dialysis). 6) Recheck for rebound. The major error is treating the number with insulin, seeing K improve, and forgetting that essentially none of the potassium has left the body.
Its sole job is electrophysiologic membrane stabilization while you fix the potassium. Effect is temporary (~30-60 min). Potassium toxicity can recur.

Insulin and albuterol redistribute K intracellularly — temporarily. When effects wear off, K redistributes extracellularly unless it has been urinated, bound/excreted, or dialyzed out. Always ask: how is potassium actually leaving this body?

Falsely elevated K from hemolysis, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, prolonged tourniquet, fist clenching, traumatic draw. Confirm if ECG and clinical picture don't fit — but treat immediately if unstable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
items: Waiting for a repeat K before treating a patient with K 7.4 + bradycardia or QRS widening.
Being reassured by a normal ECG — !!≥50%!! of severe hyperkalemia has no classic ECG changes.
Giving only 1g calcium gluconate to a peri-arrest patient — standard calcium gluconate dose for hyperkalemia is 3g (30 mL), not 1g.
Confusing 1g CaCl₂ and 1g calcium gluconate: 1g Chloride = 3g gluconate.
Ordering albuterol 2.5 mg neb: that is a bronchodilator dose, not a hyperkalemia dose (use 10-20 mg).
Monitoring glucose for only 1 hour after insulin — delayed hypoglycemia peaks at ~2h and risk persists to 6h.
Repeatedly giving insulin rounds without arranging any potassium elimination — the K is still in the body.
Giving bicarbonate reflexively to every hyperkalemic patient without meaningful metabolic acidosis.
Avoiding LR simply because it contains potassium — large-volume NS can worsen acidosis and K shift.
Relying on SPS/Kayexalate as acute emergency therapy — slow, unpredictable, poor evidence, bowel risk.
Calling nephrology only after medical therapy has failed in an anuric ESRD patient with K 7.0.
Ignoring the medication list — ACEi/ARB/MRA/TMP/NSAIDs are very common contributors.

↓ deep tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia)

Cardiac rhythm: irregular rhythm if arrhythmia

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Mg2+ — always check Mg), urine K+ (spot K/Cr ratio to assess renal vs GI losses)
-**Orders:** IV access, telemetry (QT prolongation, U-waves), continuous SpO2, replace Mg2+ first (required for K+ repletion)
**Stat:** BMP (K, Cr), Mg (always check: hypoK refractory if Mg low), ECG
**ECG findings:** Flattened T waves: ST depression: prominent U waves: QT prolongation: torsades/VT/VF if K <2.5
**Workup:** Urine K (>20 mEq/L = renal loss, <20 = extrarenal), urine Cl, ABG/VBG, phos, calcium
**If refractory:** Urine K/Cr ratio, plasma renin/aldosterone (hyperaldosteronism), TSH, cortisol
Check & replace Mg first: give MgSO4 2g IV if Mg <2.0
**Mild (3.0–3.5):** KCl 40 mEq PO. Recheck in 4h.
**Moderate (2.5–3.0):** KCl 40 mEq PO + 10–20 mEq/h IV. Place on tele.
--Max peripheral IV rate: 10 mEq/h (higher rates cause phlebitis: use central line)
--Each 10 mEq IV KCl raises serum K by ~0.1 mEq/L
Continue replacement until K >4.0
Recheck BMP q2–4h during active replacement until K >3.5
Start PO replacement once K >3.0 & tolerating PO
Txt underlying cause: hold diuretic, treat GI losses
--For pts on digoxin: maintain K >4.0 (hypoK potentiates dig toxicity)
Consider K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone, amiloride)
Dietary counseling: potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach)

drugs.name: KCl (oral)
drugs.notes: Preferred for mild-moderate. Take with food to reduce GI upset.

drugs.name: KCl (IV)
drugs.dose: 10–20 mEq/h peripheral, up to 40 mEq/h central
drugs.contraindications: Hyperkalemia, anuria; administer via infusion only (never IV push)
drugs.notes: Max 10 mEq/h peripherally. Central line for 20 mEq/hr. Always on tele.

drugs.name: MgSO4
drugs.notes: Replace Mg first: hypoK refractory if Mg low. Target Mg >2.0.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.notes: Ksparing diuretic. For chronic hypoK from diuretic use or hyperaldosteronism.

items: Acuity: acute (<48h: marathon runners, psychogenic polydipsia, postop, ecstasy) vs chronic (>48h: most inpts). Acute can corrected faster; chronic = high ODS risk
**Meds**: thiazides (most common drug cause), SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, NSAIDs, desmopressin, cyclophosphamide, sulfonylureas, bupropion, opioids
**Volume losses**: vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, poor PO, NG suction, burns
**Volume overload**: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure
**Pulm/CNS dz**: PNA, lung cancer (SIAD), brain tumor, SAH, meningitis, postop state
**Endocrine**: hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency ( must r/o: both cause hyponatremia & mimic SIAD)
Alcohol use, malnutrition, liver dz: ↑ ODS risk
**Baseline Na trend**: how fast did it drop? Prior Na values critical for determining chronicity
**Recent IVF**: hypotonic fluids (D5W, 0.45% NS) worsens hyponatremia

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Symptoms scale with severity and rate of fall — mild (nausea, headache) to severe (seizures, coma); volume status (hypo/eu/hypervolemic) and acuity (acute vs chronic) determine the correction strategy
Symptom severity determines urgency:
Severe: seizures, obtundation/coma (GCS <8), cardiorespiratory distress, vomiting
Moderate: confusion, headache, nausea without vomiting
Mild: gait disturbance, falls, concentration difficulty, cognitive deficits
Sxemerge below Na ~120 mEq/L, but depend on rate of decline
Volume status assessment Narrows DDx:
--Hypovolemic: dry mucous membranes, ↓ skin turgor, tachycardia, orthostasis, flat JVP
--Euvolemic: clinically nl. volume: think SIAD, hypothyroid, adrenal insufficiency
--Hypervolemic: edema, JVD, crackles, ascites: think CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure
Neuro exam: mentation, focal deficits (r/o CNS cause), seizure activity

sections.title: Correction Rate & ODS Prevention
items: Max correction rates: **≤10 mEq/L in first 24h**, ≤8 mEq/L per 24h reafter, until Na ≥130
**K correction counts toward Na correction**: every 1 mEq K repleted raises Na ~1 mEq/L. Factor this in
High ODS risk: (aim for even slower correction, **≤6-8** mEq/24h): Na <105, chronic hyponatremia, alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, cirrhosis, burns
**Autocorrection risk**: when cause of hyponatremia resolves (e.g., hypovolemia corrected with IVF, drug stopped), ADH drops: sudden massive free water excretion: rapid Na rise
**DDAVP clamp strategy**: if autocorrection risk is high, start DDAVP 2mcg IV q8h proactively + restrict free water to <1L/day + controlled 3% NaCl if needed
Monitor Na q1-2h after intervention, then q4-6h. Do NOT set and forget
If Na overcorrects: STOP all saline. Give D5W 6-10 mL/kg over 1-2h. Give DDAVP 2mcg IV. Recheck Na q1-2h. Goal: relower Na back to safe trajectory
ODS sx appear **2-6 days after** overcorrection: dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, AMS, locked-in syndrome. MRI may delayed. May be irreversible
Give thiamine 100mg IV daily if AUD or malnutrition risk

pairs.value: Hypotonic (<275) = true hyponatremia: proceed. Isotonic (275-295) = pseudohyponatremia. Hypertonic (>295) = dilutional (hyperglycemia, mannitol)
<100 mOsm = dilute urine, **ADH OFF** (psychogenic polydipsia, beer potomania, low solute intake, reset osmostat). >100 mOsm = ADH present: step 3
<20-30 mEq/L = **RAAS ON**: hypovolemic (GI losses, 3rdspacing) or hypervolemic (CHF, cirrhosis). >20-30 mEq/L = SIAD, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, renal failure, diuretics

Thiazides, cerebral salt wasting, RTA, mineralocorticoid deficiency, osmotic diuresis
SIAD (most common inpt cause), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, psychogenic polydipsia (UOsm <100), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine)

Adrenal insufficiency (random cortisol, ACTH stim) & hypothyroidism (TSH): both mimic SIAD but require specific tx

items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (Na+, Cr, glucose, BUN), serum osmolality, urine Na+, urine osmolality, TSH, cortisol (if adrenal insufficiency suspected)
-**Orders:** IV access, strict I&Os (free water restriction if SIADH), continuous SpO2, telemetry, neurology consult (if severe/symptomatic)
Severe sx (seizures, coma, resp distress): 3% NaCl 150mL IV bolus over 20 min: can repeat q20min up to 3-4 times. Each 100 mL raises Na ~2 mEq/L. Goal: ↑ Na by 4-6 mEq/L to stop sx
Moderate sx (confusion, headache, nausea): 3% NaCl 150mL IV over 20 min x1. Recheck Na at 1h. May repeat if no improvement
Correction rate limits: ≤10 mEq/L in first 24h, ≤8 mEq/L per 24h reafter. Overcorrection: osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)
Check Na q1-2h after hypertonic saline bolus, then q4-6h during correction
**DDAVP clamp (2mcg IV q8h)**: consider if baseline Na <120 & cause likely to autocorrect (resolved hypovolemia, water intoxication, reversible SIAD). Prevents uncontrolled free water excretion
Identify & treat underlying cause: volume status, meds, infection, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism
--**BMP:** Na, K ( hypoK ↑ ODS risk: correct K simultaneously), glucose (correct Na for hyperglycemia), BUN/Cr
--**Serum osmolality:** First step. Hypotonic (<275) = true hyponatremia. If not hypotonic: pseudohyponatremia or hypertonic
--**Urine osmolality:** <100 = ADH suppressed (polydipsia, beer potomania). >100 = ADH active: check UNa
--**Urine sodium:** <20-30 = effective volume depletion or edematous state. >20-30 = SIAD, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, renal dz
--**TSH:** r/o hypothyroidism as cause
--**AM cortisol ± ACTH stim:** r/o adrenal insufficiency: critical before labeling as SIAD
--**Uric acid:** Low in SIAD (↑ uric acid excretion). Elevated in hypovolemia
--**LFTs, albumin:** If cirrhosis suspected
--**CXR:** Lung pathology causing SIAD (PNA, cancer, TB)
--**CT head:** If CNS cause suspected (tumor, SAH, meningitis) or if AMS without clear cause

sections.title: SIAD (SIADH) Management
items: **Dx of exclusion**: hypotonic hyponatremia, UOsm >100, UNa >20-30, euvolemic, nl. renal function (GFR >20-25), adrenal & thyroid function nl.
**Common causes**: pulm dz (PNA, cancer, COPD), CNS dz (SAH, tumor, meningitis, stroke), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, opioids, cyclophosphamide, MDMA), pain, nausea, postop state
Treat underlying cause first: stop offending drug, treat infection, etc.
Fluid restrict: 500-1000 mL/day (first line but compliance is poor, esp in inpts receiving IV meds/nutrition)
Oral **urea 15-60g/day**: emerging as preferred tx. Osmotic diuresis. Mix with juice
**Salt tabs 1-3g PO TID** with meals: less potent alternative
**Furosemide 20mg q6h + salt tabs/urea: ↑ free water excretion**
Avoid NS in SIAD: if UOsm > NS osmolality (308 mOsm), NS worsens hyponatremia (kidney retains water, excretes Na)
Vaptans (tolvaptan): unpredictable aquaresis, overcorrection risk, hepatotoxicity. Not suggested in most ICU settings
**SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin 25mg/day)**: emerging option for chronic SIAD. Promotes osmotic diuresis

drugs.name: 2-3% NaCl (hypertonic saline)
drugs.dose: 150mL IV bolus over 20 min. May repeat q20min x3-4 for severe sx. **Each 100mL= ↑ Na ~2 mEq/L**
drugs.route: IV (peripheral OK for boluses; central for prolonged infusion)
drugs.contraindications: Hypervolemic hyponatremia (relative: use cautiously with diuretics in CHF/cirrhosis)
drugs.notes: Only for symptomatic hyponatremia. Goal: ↑ Na 4-6 mEq/L to resolve acute sx. Do NOT target nl. Na. Recheck Na after each bolus

drugs.name: DDAVP (desmopressin)
drugs.notes: DDAVP clamp: prevents overcorrection by locking ADH on. Use if Na <120 & cause can autocorrect. Also use to relower Na if overcorrecting (with D5W)

drugs.name: D5W (5% dextrose in water)
drugs.notes: For overcorrection rescue: free water to relower Na. Use with DDAVP. Goal: bring Na back down to safe correction trajectory

drugs.name: Oral urea
drugs.dose: 15-60 g/day PO (start ~30g daily, mix with juice to mask taste)
drugs.contraindications: Hepatic encephalopathy, severe hepatic failure, GI intolerance
drugs.notes: Emerging first line for chronic SIAD. Osmotic diuretic: promotes free water excretion. Better tolerated than extreme fluid restriction

drugs.name: nl. saline (0.9% NaCl)
drugs.notes: For hypovolemic hyponatremia only. Corrects volume depletion: turns off ADH: Na rises. Caution: worsens SIAD (Na in NS < UOsm: net free water retention)

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: For hypervolemic hyponatremia (CHF, cirrhosis): promotes free water excretion. Can combine with salt tabs or oral urea in SIAD. Replace K aggressively

drugs.name: KCl (potassium chloride)
drugs.notes: **Correct K simultaneously: K repletion raises Na** (K is osmotically active). HypoK ↑ ODS risk. Every 1 mEq K given ≈ raises Na by ~1 mEq (counts toward correction limit)

pairs.value: Na <135 mEq/L. Mild: 130-134. Moderate: 125-129. Severe: <125

Mentation: AMS, lethargy, obtundation/coma (severe)
Volume assessment
Abd exam: distension (ileus)
EKG: short QTc
MSK: proximal weakness, hyporeflexia
Bone tenderness at metastatic sites

pairs.value: Most common outpt cause. PTH inappropriately nl. or elevated; lownl. phosphorus. Usually adenoma, less commonly hyperplasia or MEN syndrome.
Most common inpt cause. SCC (lung, head/neck), renal cell, bladder, breast, ovarian cancers. PTH suppressed; PTHrP elevated.
Breast cancer, multiple myeloma, bony metastases: direct bone resorption with high calcium &bone pain.
Lymphoma & some granulomatous or hematologic processes increase 1,25OH vitamin D.
Vitamin D intoxication, excessive calcitriol, granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB, fungal disease): increased GI calcium absorption.
Thiazides, lithium, calcium carbonate or vitamin A excess, Ca/Vit D supplements, teriparatide; review OTCs & antacids.
Hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, pheochromocytoma;milder than malignancy or primary hyperPTH.
Immobilization, Paget disease, rhabdo recovery, advanced CKD/transplantrelated hypercalcemia, milkalkali syndrome.
Lifelong mild hypercalcemia with low urine calcium; benign &mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism.
High albumin or dehydration can raise total calcium; confirm with corrected calcium or ionized calcium.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (Ca2+, Cr, K+, PO4), ionized calcium, PTH, PTHrP, 25-OH vitamin D, CBC, SPEP (if MM suspected)
-**Orders:** IV access, aggressive IV fluids (NS, 200-500 mL/hr initially), Foley (strict I&Os), telemetry (short QT), continuous SpO2
--**Ionized calcium:** Most accurate: not affected by albumin. >5.6 mg/dL confirms hypercalcemia
--**PTH:** Should be suppressed (<20 pg/mL) in malignancy. If elevated: primary hyperparathyroidism
--**PTHrP:** Elevated in hypercalcemia of malignancy
--**BMP, Mg, Phos:** check renal function, coelectrolyte abnormalities
--**ECG:** Shortened QT, ST changes, Osborn waves (severe). Telemetry if Ca >14
--**25OH vitamin D, 1,25OH vitamin D:** Elevated 1,25OH in calcitriolmed. (lymphoma)
Start aggressive **NS** and track UOP; use loop diuretic only if overloaded
--titrate to UOP 200-300 mL/h (watch for retention; overload)
Give **calcitonin 4 units/kg SC or IV q12h** for rapid but shortterm Ca lowering
--Continue calcitonin q12h for first 48h (stop if Ca returns to normal)(bridge to bisphosphonate effect)
Add antiresorptive txt: **zoledronic acid 4mg IV** preferred; use **denosumab** if bisphosphonaterefractory or renal impairment
--If calcitriol med. cause is likely, add prednisone; correct Mg/K and stop Ca/vit D, thiazides, and lithium
Treat the cause in parallel: malignancy, hyperPTH, granulomatous dz, or meds
Repeat iCal q6-8h until trending down & <12 mg/dL
Recheck Cal 2-4 days after bisphosphonate: peak effect at 4-7 days
Correct hypomagnesemia (Mg <2.0) & hypokalemia as needed
Monitor renal function daily: saline infusion + bisphosphonates can affect kidneys
Definitive tx: tumordirected therapy (chemo, radiation, surgery)
Hypercalcemia of malignancy suggests poor prognosis: median survival 3-6 months = Discuss goals of care

drugs.name: nl. saline
drugs.notes: First-line tx. Restores intravascular volume & promotes renal calcium excretion. Target 3-6L in 24h.

drugs.name: Calcitonin (salmon)
drugs.notes: Fastest onset (2-4h). Lowers Ca by 1-2 mg/dL. Tachyphylaxis develops in 48-72h: bridge to bisphosphonates.

drugs.name: Zoledronic acid
drugs.notes: Preferred bisphosphonate. Onset 2-4 days, duration 2-4 weeks. More effective & faster than pamidronate.

drugs.name: Pamidronate
drugs.notes: Alternative bisphosphonate. 90mg dose for Ca >13.5. Slower infusion needed for renal protection.

drugs.name: Denosumab
drugs.notes: For bisphosphonaterefractory hypercalcemia or renal impairment. Onset 4-10 days.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.notes: Effective for calcitriolmed. hypercalcemia: lymphoma, myeloma, granulomatous disease.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: Only AFTER adequate volume resuscitation. Promotes calciuresis. Do NOT use before hydration: worsens dehydration.

Position supine or Trendelenburg.

Pericardial effusion/tamponade: ESRD pts accumulate effusions silently — POCUS every time the cause is unclear.
Do NOT stop dialysis and call it resolved without identifying the cause — recurrence is likely.
Holding antihypertensives before dialysis (especially long-acting) prevents many preventable episodes.
Cool dialysate (35-36°C) significantly reduces intradialytic hypotension by promoting vasoconstriction.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CBC (serial Hgb), coags, type & crossmatch
-**Orders:** IV access (non-access arm), vascular surgery consult, CXR if catheter-related
**Direct firm pressure**: apply continuously for at least 5-10 min — do not release to check.
Stop dialysis blood pump and clamp lines if circuit issue.
If pressure fails after 15-20 min: call vascular surgery — do NOT attempt to tourniquet a functional fistula without surgical guidance.
**Tourniquet use**: only as a life-saving measure for exsanguinating hemorrhage; risks permanent access loss.
Reverse heparin with protamine sulfate: 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given in last 2-4 hours (max 50 mg).
**Resuscitate**: IV fluids, MTP for active bleed or hemodynamically unstable.
--Activate MTP if massive hemorrhage.
Expanding hematoma threatening access or limb: emergent vascular surgery for surgical decompression or repair.

pairs.value: Loss of thrill/bruit over AV fistula or graft. (1)**Call vascular surgery +/-IR** for thrombectomy or thrombolysis. Time-sensitive: best outcomes within hours.

Very high-flow AV access (brachial-based fistulas) → ↑ venous return → cardiac dilation → HF symptoms. **Access banding or ligation** may be needed.
Inability to achieve adequate blood flow for dialysis in a patient needing urgent RRT. Try repositioning, fibrinolytic lock (tPA 1-2 mg per lumen), or IR-guided exchange.

items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CBC, BMP, blood cultures, CRP, ESR, lactate, vancomycin trough (pre-3rd dose), Blood Cx x2 before antibiotics.
-**Orders:** IV antibiotics STAT, echocardiogram (if S. aureus), catheter removal decision, vascular surgery consult
Start empiric vancomycin STAT — dialysis-dosed (see below); add gram-negative coverage if septic shock or immunocompromised.
**If septic shock**: IV fluids 30 mL/kg (use 500 mL aliquots in ESRD — recheck frequently), vasopressors if MAP <65.
Catheter removal: remove infected catheter ASAP in bacteremia + hemodynamic instability, fungemia, or no clinical improvement in 48-72h. Replace at new site (avoid guidewire exchange if possible).
**Salvage attempt**: temporary catheter removal + antibiotic lock therapy only if catheter is essential and patient is hemodynamically stable with non-Staph aureus, non-fungal infection.
**Infected AV graft**: vascular surgery consult STAT — synthetic graft infection typically requires surgical excision + revascularization.
**Infected AV fistula**: IV antibiotics; surgery if abscess, mycotic aneurysm, or failure to respond.
Echocardiogram for all Staph aureus bacteremia (endocarditis risk 20-30%)
**Duration**:CRBSI 2-4 weeks IV; endocarditis 6 weeks; osteomyelitis 6+ weeks.

drugs.name: Vancomycin (dialysis-dosed)
drugs.dose: Loading dose: 25 mg/kg IV (max 3g); maintenance: 500-1000 mg post-dialysis session
drugs.notes: Gold standard for MRSA in dialysis patients. Infuse over 1-2h to avoid red man syndrome. Check vancomycin AUC/MIC or trough. Renally eliminated — dosed by dialysis schedule.

drugs.name: Daptomycin
drugs.notes: Alternative to vancomycin for MRSA CRBSI. Particularly useful if vancomycin MIC creep. Monitor CK levels.

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.notes: For MSSA (methicillin-sensitive S. aureus). Superior to vancomycin for MSSA — de-escalate if susceptible.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
drugs.dose: 3.375g IV q8h extended infusion (adjust for ESRD)
drugs.notes: Gram-negative and anaerobic coverage; add if bowel source, infected graft with perioperative contamination, or septic shock.

pairs.value: Fever or rigors during or after dialysis, erythema or purulence at catheter exit site, positive blood cultures with no other source. Most common organism: S. aureus (including MRSA).
Erythema, warmth, fluctuance, or purulent drainage over graft. May present with systemic sepsis. Surgical emergency — infected synthetic graft typically requires excision.
Less common than graft infection; usually presents as localized cellulitis or abscess. May respond to antibiotics alone if not thrombosed.
Staph aureus bacteremia in dialysis patients has very high rates of endocarditis (20-30%), vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis. Always get echo and monitor closely.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: Staph aureus bacteremia in dialysis patients: endocarditis rate is 20-30%.
Never guide-wire exchange an infected catheter — high risk of seeding the new catheter.
Infected synthetic AV graft almost always requires surgical excision.
Vancomycin levels in ESRD are not straightforward — dose post-dialysis and check levels systematically.
!!ESRD patients often lack fever or leukocytosis despite severe infection — low threshold to culture and treat!!.

items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+), CBC (Hgb drop), LDH, plasma free hemoglobin, haptoglobin, UA

**STOP dialysis and clamp lines** — do NOT return circuit blood to patient.
**EKG immediately**: look for hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS, PR prolongation, sine wave).

If hemodynamically unstable: ICU transfer, vasopressors as needed.
!!Figure Out Cause!!: inspect water temp, tubing for kinks, check machine alarm logs, notify biomedical engineering.
If multiple patients affected: c/f water supply contamination — alert entire dialysis unit and isolate water source.
Do not restart dialysis until cause is identified and corrected.
If repeat dialysis needed now: use a different machine and verified water supply.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.notes: Membrane stabilization for hyperkalemic EKG changes. Onset ~1-3 min. Repeat if EKG changes persist after 5 min.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.notes: Shifts K+ intracellularly. Useful adjunct; effect takes 15-30 min.

drugs.name: Insulin + Dextrose
drugs.dose: 10 units regular insulin IV + 25g D50 (1 amp) IV
drugs.notes: Most reliable K+ shift agent. Onset 20-30 min. Monitor glucose q1h.

drugs.name: Albuterol nebulized
drugs.notes: Adjunct to insulin for K+ shift. Note: standard 2.5 mg dose is inadequate for hyperkalemia — use 10-20 mg.

pairs.value: Chest pain, back pain, dyspnea, flushing, nausea — occur during or shortly after dialysis. Sudden worsening = hemolysis until proven otherwise.
Venous blood appears dark red or maroon (hemolyzed blood) rather than normal dark red. Port wine color = severe hemolysis. The most visible clue.
Massive intravascular hemolysis releases intracellular K+ — can cause sudden life-threatening hyperkalemia mid-session in a patient whose K+ was previously controlled.
Dialysate temperature >42°C causes thermal hemolysis. Machine temperature alarm failure. Patient feels hot, diaphoretic, with burning pain.
Dialysate sodium <120 mEq/L causes osmotic lysis of RBCs. Machine proportioning error or concentrated solution error.

Water treatment failure: chloramines from municipal water supply or copper from corroded pipes cause oxidative hemolysis. May affect multiple patients simultaneously — cluster of cases = water supply problem.
Severe tubing kink, occluded bloodline, high pump speed through narrow line → mechanical shear stress on RBCs.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: NEVER return hemolyzed circuit blood to the patient — free hemoglobin + hyperkalemic plasma can cause immediate cardiac arrest.
Multiple patients affected at the same time = water supply contamination event — treat as a unit-wide emergency.
Hemolysis-induced hyperkalemia can be sudden and severe even in patients who came in with a controlled K+ — EKG is essential.
Dark or port-wine colored blood in the venous chamber is the key visual clue — inspect the circuit immediately.
Chloramine poisoning is the most dangerous water contamination event: methemoglobin + hemolysis; consider methylene blue if methemoglobinemia is present.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (BUN, Na+), serum osmolality, glucose
-**Orders:** CT head, stop dialysis, lorazepam if seizing, hypertonic saline if cerebral edema, ICU
**Mild symptoms (headache, nausea)**: reduce blood flow rate by 30-50%; reduce dialysate clearance; monitor closely.
**Moderate symptoms (confusion, disorientation)**: stop dialysis; give IV mannitol 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline; monitor neuro status.
**Severe symptoms (seizure, coma)**: stop dialysis immediately; lorazepam 4 mg IV for seizures; hypertonic saline or mannitol for cerebral edema; urgent CT head; neurology + ICU consult.
**Airway management**: intubate if GCS ≤8 or unable to protect airway.
Do not restart dialysis until patient is stabilized and a plan for safer gradual dialysis is established.
**Prevention**: for new ESRD patients with BUN >100-150 mg/dL, use shorter initial sessions (2h max), slow blood flow rates (150-200 mL/min), and low-efficiency membranes.
Add mannitol prophylactically (1 g/kg IV) during first dialysis for very high BUN patients.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 2-4 mg IV; repeat q5-10 min PRN (max 8-10 mg)
drugs.notes: First-line for active seizure in DDS. Benzodiazepine of choice; rapid onset.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.dose: 1 g/kg IV over 20-30 min (prophylactic or therapeutic)
drugs.notes: Raises plasma osmolality to counteract brain-plasma gradient. Use prophylactically for first sessions in BUN >150.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 23.4%
drugs.dose: 30 mL IV bolus via central line
drugs.notes: For severe cerebral edema or herniation. Rapidly raises plasma osmolality. Central line required.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3%
drugs.notes: Peripheral-safe alternative to 23.4%. Target Na 145-155 mEq/L for refractory ICP.

pairs.value: Neurological symptoms caused by rapid osmotic shift: rapid removal of urea lowers plasma osmolality faster than brain osmolality → water shifts into brain cells → cerebral edema.
Most common during first few dialysis sessions in a patient with severely elevated BUN (>100-150 mg/dL). Can occur with overly aggressive clearance in any session.
Mild: headache, nausea, blurred vision, restlessness. Moderate: confusion, disorientation, muscle cramps. Severe: seizures, coma, cerebral herniation, death.
Plasma urea cleared faster than brain urea → plasma osmolality drops rapidly → osmotic gradient draws water into brain → intracranial hypertension and cerebral edema.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: Prevention > treatment — use slow, gentle dialysis sessions for new ESRD with high BUN.
DDS vs. uremic encephalopathy: uremia improves with dialysis; DDS worsens with aggressive dialysis.
Always rule out hypoglycemia first — fingerstick glucose takes 30 seconds.
CT head: for new focal deficit or severe headache — concurrent ICH or stroke must be excluded.
!!Mannitol prophylaxis!! = first dialysis session for BUN >150 is a simple and effective preventive strategy.

pairs.value: Onset within minutes of starting dialysis. Pruritis, urticaria, flushing, bronchospasm, hypotension, angioedema. IgE-mediated or bradykinin-mediated (especially with ACE inhibitors + AN69 membranes). **Stop dialysis, do NOT return blood**.
Chest and back pain 20-40 min into dialysis **without anaphylaxis features**. Mechanism unclear. Usually resolves with slowing of dialysis. Less dangerous than Type A.
Classic combination for severe anaphylactoid reaction (bradykinin accumulation). Ask about ACE inhibitor use before dialysis. Hold ACE inhibitor or switch dialyzer membrane.
Stop dialysis, do NOT return circuit blood. **Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM** (first-line). Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV. IV fluids and vasopressors if hypotensive.
Air enters venous blood line via disconnected tubing, empty IV bag run dry into dialysis line, cracked line, or improper priming. Dialysis machine venous air detector should alarm but can fail.
Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cough, cyanosis, hypotension, altered consciousness, mill wheel murmur on auscultation. Can be rapidly fatal with large air volumes.
Clamp venous blood line immediately. Do NOT return blood to patient. Place patient left lateral decubitus with head down (Durant maneuver). 100% O2 via NRB. CPR if cardiac arrest.
Left lateral decubitus + Trendelenburg position traps air in the apex of the right ventricle, preventing it from entering the pulmonary outflow tract. Hold this position during resuscitation.
Hypokalemia (aggressive dialysis with low-K+ bath), hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, rapid fluid shifts, intradialytic hypotension causing coronary ischemia, air embolism.
Standard ACLS. Stop dialysis. Defibrillation and cardioversion are safe with dialysis access in place. Get EKG, electrolytes. Correct K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ as needed.
Using dialysate K+ <2 mEq/L in patients on digoxin or baseline hypokalemia significantly increases arrhythmia risk. Use K+ 3-4 mEq/L dialysate bath.
ESRD patients have very high risk of cardiac arrest during dialysis. Consider ICD evaluation if recurrent ventricular arrhythmias. Discuss with cardiology.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Ca2+, Mg2+), ABG, tryptase (if anaphylaxis suspected)
-**Orders:** EKG, stop dialysis, 100% O2, epinephrine if anaphylaxis, left lateral decubitus if air embolism, ACLS if arrest
**Anaphylaxis**: stop dialysis, clamp lines, do NOT return blood. Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM thigh. Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV. 1L NS IV. Vasopressors if refractory.
**Air embolism**: clamp venous line immediately. Left lateral Trendelenburg. 100% O2 by non-rebreather. CPR if arrest. Consider aspiration of air via catheter if massive.
**Arrhythmia**: standard ACLS, stop dialysis. EKG. Correct electrolytes (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+). Defibrillation safe with access in place.
**Cardiac arrest on dialysis:** standard CPR and ACLS. Check for reversible causes: hyperkalemia, tamponade, tension PTX, MI, air embolism.

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.dose: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (thigh); repeat q5-15 min PRN
drugs.notes: First-line for anaphylaxis. If refractory: epinephrine gtt 0.05-0.3 mcg/kg/min IV. Do not delay.

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine
drugs.contraindications: Acute angle-closure glaucoma, BPH, MAO inhibitor use within 14 days
drugs.notes: Adjunct to epinephrine for anaphylaxis. Does not replace epinephrine.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated infection (relative); caution in DM, GI bleed
drugs.notes: Prevents biphasic anaphylaxis reaction. Slow onset; not immediate therapy. Adjunct to epinephrine.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.notes: For hypocalcemia-triggered arrhythmia or hyperkalemia-related EKG changes during dialysis.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: For torsades or hypomagnesemia-related arrhythmia. Give during or immediately after dialysis if possible.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP, CBC, BNP, albumin, UA (protein/Cr ratio if nephrotic range)
-**Orders:** CXR, IV access, daily weight, strict I&Os, bilateral LE dopplers (if asymmetric edema)
1. Sit pt upright and start O2. If SCAPE/flash pulmonary edema is causing marked dyspnea or hypoxemia, start NIPPV early.
2. Start nitroglycerin for preload/afterload reduction. Use higher urgency when severe HTN is driving the edema.
3.IV loop diuretic furosemide 40-80 mg if volume overloaded or known CHF: about 2.5× the home PO loop dose.
4. Recheck WOB, BP, urine output, and response. If hypotension, poor perfusion, or worsening respiratory failure develops= cardiogenic shock.

drugs.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
drugs.notes: First-line for cardiac edema. Can escalate to drip 5-40 mg/hr if refractory.

drugs.name: Metolazone
drugs.notes: Thiazide-like — synergistic w/ loop diuretics for refractory edema. Watch electrolytes.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.notes: Potassium-sparing. Adds mortality benefit in systolic CHF (RALES trial). Avoid if K >5.0 or CrCl <30.
